title: Growing sorrel
subtitle: A tangy perennial leaf grown almost year-round in UK conditions.
excerpt: Sorrel is a perennial grown for its sharp, lemony leaves, available from early spring through to hard frosts. It grows in partial shade, tolerates poor soil, and asks very little once established. Cut the flower stems out to extend the harvest season.
sourceNotes: Cultivation notes from Joy Larkcom, Grow Your Own Vegetables (1976). French sorrel variety information from RHS Plant Selector data. Oxalic acid note widely documented in food science literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: When a plant switches from producing leaves to producing flowers and seed. Bolting is triggered by day length, temperature, or stress. Sorrel, lettuce, and spinach all bolt in long summer days. Remove flower stems as they appear to delay bolting and extend the leaf harvest.

content.text: Sorrel is a hardy perennial with a sharp, lemony flavour from oxalic acid. The leaves are available from March until hard frost, and the plant is often still green in mild winters. It is one of the few vegetables that grows and produces usefully in partial shade.

Common sorrel (Rumex acetosa) is the UK native with large leaves and a strong sharp flavour. French sorrel (Rumex scutatus) has smaller, shield-shaped leaves and a milder flavour. Both are perennial. French sorrel is lower-growing and useful between other plants.

Sow seed in pots or direct in March to April, or in August. Germination is fast in warm soil. Plant out 30 cm apart. Sorrel tolerates most soils except waterlogged ground. Divide established plants in autumn to make new ones.
Pick individual outer leaves from spring to autumn. The leaves are best when young and tender. In late spring and summer, sorrel sends up flower stems: this is

. Cut flower stems out as they appear to keep the plant producing leaves rather than seed. If the plant looks exhausted in midsummer, cut it to 10 cm and it will regrow fresh leaves within three weeks.
Divide the clump every three to four years when it becomes overcrowded. Replant the outer sections and compost the woody centre.

attrs.title: Using sorrel in cooking
attrs.body: Sorrel wilts down to a fraction of its raw volume when cooked and turns an olive-green colour. Use it in sauces, soups, and omelettes rather than as a salad base in large quantities. A small handful of raw leaves adds a sharp note to a mixed salad. The sharpness softens when cooked with eggs or cream. As with spinach and Good King Henry, people with kidney stones are advised to eat it only occasionally.
